note: The pre-registered fifth-batch SYO case (event 264, Broomhill/Crookes, 5147x6427 px) run with --native-resolution was OOM-killed by the 1.5 GiB cgroup cap after 128 s and wrote no result; that outcome is preserved as 'killed'. The verifier's --native-resolution mode passes the decoded GIF straight to analyze()/service.geographic_registration, bypassing the 4096-px working cap that the real service applies to every upload. This separate run applies the service's 4096-px working cap (image 3280x4096) and nothing else; it is the only such run (run once, not repeated).

serviceCapRun.command: systemd-run --user --scope -q -p MemoryMax=1.5G -p MemorySwapMax=0 -p CPUQuota=100% /usr/bin/time -v python3 -B verify_new_areas.py --native-resolution --service-cap --host https://www.syo.routegadget.co.uk --events 264
serviceCapRun.verifierChange: Copy of tools/verify_new_areas.py at frozen 785874a with one added flag --service-cap: when the source long side exceeds 4096 px, the decoded image is resized to round(side*4096/long_side) with cv2.INTER_AREA, as dirmap.images.read_map_image (MAX_WORKING_SIDE=4096) does for an upload, and the world file is composed with that function's workingToSource pixel mapping [[sx,0,.5sx-.5],[0,sy,.5sy-.5]]. No other change. The row's 'upscale' stays 1.0 because the cap is folded into the world file, not into the factor.

scope:
First-time automatic registration on maps of places DirMap has never seen.

Every classroom so far brought a map of a new place. This check imitates
that: for each published orienteering map it downloads the OpenStreetMap
reference of a viewport around the sheet (as a teacher adding a place would),
then runs recognition and the automatic geographic registration exactly once,
with no tuning per place. Each map comes from a RouteGadget server whose
organisers georeferenced it with a world file. The file frames the teacher's
viewport and, by default, normalises resolution toward classroom-photo
scale. Use --native-resolution to retain original pixels instead. Matching
receives neither the world-file transform nor its landmarks; the resulting
pose is measured against that transform afterwards.

World files are the organisers' own georeferencing (usually three manually
picked points), so they carry a few metres of error themselves. The check
classifies an outcome as correct, wrong (dangerous: a confident fit far from
the world file) or refused. It is not a field accuracy measurement.
